data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism is internally self-contradictory: it claims the preference for corroboration operates 'without invoking induction,' yet characterizes the selected theory as the 'best bet available.' A 'bet,' by definition, encodes an expectation about future payoff—here, that a theory surviving severe tests will continue to perform well. The target itself concedes in its main claim that this reduces rational action to 'a gamble on the severity of past tests.' But a gamble that expects past test-severity to bear on future performance is precisely an inductive inference (an assumption that the future will resemble the past in the relevant respect). The target's own countercondition flags this: 'If preference implies an expectation of future performance, it functionally reintroduces probability regardless of the label.' Yet the mechanism simultaneously disavows induction and embraces the language of betting, making the defense incoherent rather than merely costly. Furthermore, the mechanism's final sentence—'It follows that the underlying structure was never relevant to the outcome at all'—is a non sequitur that, taken at face value, destroys the argument's own basis: if the underlying structure (the relationship between corroboration and verisimilitude) is irrelevant to the outcome, then there is no reason to prefer the better-corroborated theory at all, and the methodological rule is arbitrary.
